result.markdown: --- title: "Lecture 7" execute: freeze: auto # re-render only when source changes format: revealjs: theme: serif incremental: true preview-links: auto chalkboard: true margin: 0 width: 1080 engine: julia julia: exeflags: ["--project=../PopGen25"] bibliography: references.bib --- ## Quantitative trait evolution Now that we have a better feeling for how all of the different processes impact the evolution in alleles, it's worth thinking about quantitative traits in general. . . . Today we'll talk about how genetic variation for traits is distributed, and what this tells us about their evolution. . . . We'll talk about how we can identify causal alleles for traits, and why sometimes that is either impossible, or extra complicated. . . . We'll end by considering the *ultimate* trait - fitness, and how fitness changes as populations evovle (and what that can teach us about evolution of reproductive isolation, hybridization, etc.) ## Last time Last week we talked about the Breeder's equation. $$ R = S h^2 = S \frac{V_A}{V_P} $$ . . . This equation describes how a trait changes based on changes in the average among those who mated vs the whole population, and how much of that change is heritable. . . . We did not discuss how $V_A$ changes in response to selection. ## Change in genetic variability due to selection {.smaller} Let's think through multiple cases: . . . Take directional selection, with all alleles being nice additive values for trait: decreases . . . Take directional selection, but all alleles are overdominant: decreases even faster. . . . Stabilizing selection, additive values: decreases as different alleles become fixed. . . . Stabilizing and overdominance: while no alleles are fixed, $V_A$ goes to 0. ## Remember that we care about the *additive* genetic variation ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Plots, Measures, LaTeXStrings theme(:vibrant) default(xlabelfontsize=16,ylabelfontsize=16,margins=4mm,markerstrokewidth=0,linewidth=2,dpi=400) a = bar(["aa","aA","AA"],[1,1.2,1.4],leg=false,title="Additive",color=1,ylabel="trait Z") b = bar(["aa","aA","AA"],[1,1.4,1.2],leg=false,title="Overdominant",color=2,ylabel="trait Z") c = bar(["aa","aA","AA"],[1.2,1,1.4],leg=false,title="Underdominant",color=3,ylabel="trait Z") function f_add(p); (1-p)^2*1+2*p*(1-p)*1.2+p^2*1.4; end function f_over(p); (1-p)^2*1+2*p*(1-p)*1.4+p^2*1.2; end function f_under(p); (1-p)^2*1.2+2*p*(1-p)*1+p^2*1.4; end d = plot(range(0,1,length=50),f_add,label="Additive",xlabel=L"p",ylabel=L"\bar{Z}") plot!(d,range(0,1,length=50),f_over,label="Overdominant") plot!(d,range(0,1,length=50),f_under,label="Underdominant") plot(a,b,c,d;layout=@layout[[a;b;c] d{0.7w}],size=(1000,600)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Renewing $V_A$ Mutations re-introduce genetic variation for a trait. . . . Because they are *extremely* rare when they enter the population, most change in allele frequencies leads to additive effects. . . . So, most new mutations increase additive genetic variation for a trait. . . . Long-term - $V_A$ will settle on a value depending on both new mutations and strength of selection. ## Some counter-factuals {.smaller} Just because genetic variation decreases due to selection, does not mean it disappears. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using StatsPlots, CSV, DataFrames corn_data = CSV.read("data/corn_data.txt",DataFrame,missingstring=["."]) corn_plot= plot(corn_data.YR,corn_data.IHO_2,label="High Oil Selection",xlabel="Year",ylabel="Corn Oil %",dpi=400,margins=4mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## But it *can* have limits ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} plot!(corn_data.YR,corn_data.ILO_2,label="Low Oil Selection",xlabel="Year",ylabel="Corn Oil %") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## But it *is* reversible ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} plot!(corn_data.YR,corn_data.IRHO_2,label="Reverse to high") plot!(corn_data.YR,corn_data.IRLO_2,label="Reverse to low") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Long term change re-measured It's worth considering that changing by 1% oil content may be much easier when oil content is high than when it is low. . . . We instead consider the $log(\frac{X_1}{X_2})$, where $X_1$ is the starting trait value, and $X_2$ is the ending one. . . . What's often noticed on this scale is that change is *not* linear: change might be faster initially, and slow down later. . . . Not the case in corn data! ## In oil data ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} corn_plot2 = plot(corn_data.YR[2:105],[log(corn_data.IHO_2[i])-log(corn_data.IHO_2[i-1]) for i in 2:105],label="High Oil Selection",xlabel="Year",ylabel="Fold change in oil content") plot!(corn_plot2,corn_data.YR[2:105],[log(corn_data.ILO_2[i])-log(corn_data.ILO_2[i-1]) for i in 2:105],label="Low Oil Selection") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## LTEE of fitness It *is* the case for change in fitness in Lenski's long term *E. coli* evolution. ![](https://www.science.org/cms/10.1126/science.1243357/asset/6f1f047b-9303-4c88-bc7c-ebd32d50508d/assets/graphic/342_1364_f2.jpeg){width="715"} . . . Why? ## Fisher's Geometric Model ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function circle_shape(x,y,r) θ = LinRange(0,2*π,100) x .+ r*sin.(θ), y .+ r*cos.(θ) end #Plot optimum at 0,0: population at x,y fg_plot = scatter((0,0),label="Optimum",xlabel="Trait x",ylabel="Trait y",xlim=(-1,1),ylim=(-1,1),size=(800,800)) #Plot circle of radius sqrt(x^2+y^2) centered on 0,0 scatter!(fg_plot,(sqrt(1/2),sqrt(1/2)),label="Starting pop") plot!(fg_plot,circle_shape(0,0,1),seriestype=:shape,fillalpha=0.2,label="") #Plot another circle from point x,y of radius \mu plot!(fg_plot,circle_shape(sqrt(1/2),sqrt(1/2),0.2),seriestype=:shape,fillalpha=0.2,label="") #Show overlap of the two areas? ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## When closer to optimum ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function circle_shape(x,y,r) θ = LinRange(0,2*π,100) x .+ r*sin.(θ), y .+ r*cos.(θ) end #Plot optimum at 0,0: population at x,y fg_plot2 = scatter((0,0),label="Optimum",xlabel="Trait x",ylabel="Trait y",xlim=(-1,1),ylim=(-1,1),size=(800,800)) #Plot circle of radius sqrt(x^2+y^2) centered on 0,0 scatter!(fg_plot2,(0.2,0.2),label="Starting pop") plot!(fg_plot2,circle_shape(0,0,sqrt(2*0.2^2)),seriestype=:shape,fillalpha=0.2,label="") #Plot another circle from point x,y of radius \mu plot!(fg_plot2,circle_shape(0.2,0.2,0.2),seriestype=:shape,fillalpha=0.2,label="") #Show overlap of the two areas? ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## When *really* close to optimum ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function circle_shape(x,y,r) θ = LinRange(0,2*π,100) x .+ r*sin.(θ), y .+ r*cos.(θ) end #Plot optimum at 0,0: population at x,y fg_plot3 = scatter((0,0),label="Optimum",xlabel="Trait x",ylabel="Trait y",xlim=(-1,1),ylim=(-1,1),size=(800,800)) #Plot circle of radius sqrt(x^2+y^2) centered on 0,0 scatter!(fg_plot3,(0.05,0.05),label="Starting pop") plot!(fg_plot3,circle_shape(0,0,sqrt(2*0.05^2)),seriestype=:shape,fillalpha=0.2,label="") #Plot another circle from point x,y of radius \mu plot!(fg_plot3,circle_shape(0.05,0.05,0.2),seriestype=:shape,fillalpha=0.2,label="") #Show overlap of the two areas? ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## So, expectation when adapting to new optimum When populations adapt to a new optimum, the first fixed mutations are expected to have large effects. . . . Mutations fixed later in the process have increasingly smaller effects, as large effect mutations become increasingly likely to be deleterious. . . . Vanishingly unlikely that population ever fully adapts to optimum, and will instead reach a point where selection is about as strong as drift. ## How do we detect phenotypic selection? {.smaller} Knowing if some traits are under directional or stabilizing selection might be important. . . . Could just compare many related species and see if your species of interest is "extreme" for a trait value. . . . The problem is that traits do no evolve independently - correlated change due to shared ancestry. . . . So, even if evolution is not directed, there may be differences along the phylogeny that look significant. . . . The whole field of phylogenetic comparative methods is there to help you. ## Phylogenetic comparative methods {.smaller} Easiest to show the problem using multiple trait correlations. . . . ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Phylo tree = rand(Ultrametric(40)) evolve(tree) = map_depthfirst((val, node) -> val + randn(), 0., tree, Float64) trait1 = evolve(tree) trait2 = evolve(tree) tplot=plot(tree,line_z = trait1,linewidth=4,showtips=false,title="Height") tplot2 = plot(tree,line_z = trait2,linewidth=4,showtips=false,title="Time of Flowering") t1 = trait1[length(trait1)-39:length(trait1)] t2 = trait2[length(trait2)-39:length(trait2)] t3 =scatter(t1,t2,label="",xlabel="Height",ylabel="Time of Flowering") plot(tplot,tplot2,t3,size=(1200,500);layout=@layout [[a;b] c]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## PIC example {.smaller} In this case - no actual correlation between traits (or directionality): both simulated under Brownian-Motion. . . . One simple way to account for shared history: Phylogenetically independent contrasts. . . . Calculate differences between each branch, and compare these. ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} scatter(abs.(trait1),abs.(trait2),xlabel="Contrast1",ylabel="Contrast2",leg=false,size=(1200,500)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## How can we identify genetic structure of traits? Understanding the genetic basis of adaptive traits is not as straightforward as it may seem. . . . We covered this in part already - you can look at regions with differences between closely related species for selection, but not guaranteed to link to your trait. . . . If you can interbreed - QTL. . . . If still polymorphic - GWAS. ## Genome Wide Association Studies Genome wide association studies essentially take genotypes of many individuals in a population along with their phenotypes, and return the correlation between each genotype and the phenotype of interest. . . . At its heart - simple linear regression! . . . More broadly - can take advantage of known inheritance patterns (pedigrees) to account for population structure. ## GWAS example ::: {#22 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Distributions, GLM env1 = vcat(rand(Normal(0,0.4),150),rand(Normal(2,0.1),150)) xs = vcat(rand(Normal(1,0.1),100),rand(Normal(2,0.1),100),rand(Normal(3,0.1),100)) ys1 = rand(Normal(10,0.4),300) ys2 = vcat(rand(Normal(11,1.5),100), rand(Normal(10,1.5),100), rand(Normal(9,1.5),100)) zs = vcat(rand(Normal(1,0.1),150),rand(Normal(2,0.1),150)) p_causal= scatter(xs,ys1.+env1,title="Causal SNP",xticks=([1,2,3],["aa","aA","AA"]),xlabel="Genotype",ylabel="Pod size",leg=false,marker_z = ys1.+env1) lm_causal = lm(@formula(z ~ g),DataFrame(z=ys1 .+ env1,g=xs)) plot!(p_causal,[1,2,3],predict(lm_causal,DataFrame(g=[1,2,3]))) p_random = scatter(xs,ys2.+env1,title="Non-associated",xticks=([1,2,3],["aa","aA","AA"]),xlabel="Genotype",ylabel="Pod size",leg=false,marker_z=ys2.+env1) lm_random = lm(@formula(z ~ g),DataFrame(z=ys2 .+ env1,g=xs)) plot!(p_random,[1,2,3],predict(lm_random,DataFrame(g=[1,2,3]))) plot(p_causal,p_random) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Accounting for population structure The problem with just running a linear model is that some correlations exist for other reasons. . . . LD with the actual causal locus. . . . Correlation with environmental explanatory variable. ## Back to example ::: {#24 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} p1 = plot(xs,zs,ys1.+env1,seriestype=:scatter,leg=false,xlabel="Genotype",ylabel="Environment",xticks=([1,2,3],["aa","aA","AA"]),yticks=([1,2],["Hot","Cold"]),marker_z=ys1.+env1,title="Causal";xlabelfontsize=12,ylabelfontsize=12) p2 = plot(xs,zs,ys2.+env1,seriestype=:scatter,leg=false,xlabel="Genotype",ylabel="Environment",xticks=([1,2,3],["aa","aA","AA"]),yticks=([1,2],["Hot","Cold"]),title="Not Associated",marker_z=ys2.+env1;xlabelfontsize=12,ylabelfontsize=12) plot(p1,p2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## More details Most GWAS approaches are structured as linear mixed models: $$ z = x + C + \epsilon $$ Where $x$ is the genotype at a site, $C$ is a covariate matrix, and $\epsilon$ is noise. . . . For many analyses, the covariate will be the first few PCs of a PCA of the data. . . . Ideally, these would be ancestry correlations, but as you've seen, these can be hard to estimate. ## Some things you can't account for ## Multi-trait correlations and selection We've covered the Breeder's Equation, but an equally important result is Lande's Multivariate Breeder's Equation: $$ \Delta \bar{Z} = GP^{-1}S = G \beta $$ . . . Here, $G$ is the genetic variance-covariance matrix, $P$ is the phenotypic covariance matrix and $S$ is the selection gradient. $\beta$ is the vector of directional selection gradients. $\beta$ is a fraction of the phenotypic variance that is selected. ## A quick example $$ \Delta \bar{Z} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0.6 \\ 0.6 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -0.1 \end{bmatrix} \approxeq \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1/2 \end{bmatrix} $$ ## What does that mean Traits change in proportion to genetic co-variation. . . . A trait can move in the opposite direction of its optimum, if selection on a different trait is stronger and correlations are strong. . . . Most famously: Darwin's Finches ## Darwin's Finches {.smaller} Galapagos struck by a drought in 1976. Peter and Rosemary Grant measured \~700 finches before the drought, and kept track of survivors. | Trait | Before drought average | After drought average | |-------------|------------------------|-----------------------| | Weight | 16.06 | 17.13 | | Bill length | 10.63 | 10.95 | | Bill depth | 9.21 | 9.70 | . . . From the first glance - looks like positive selection on all three traits. . . . If we account for genetic covariance in traits, we can calculate $\beta$. ## Inferred selection | Trait | $\beta$ | |-------------|---------| | Weight | 0.477 | | Bill length | -0.144 | | Bill depth | 0.528 | . . . Because bill length and depth are highly correlated, stronger selection wins out. ## Across species variation ![Beausoleil et al. 2023](https://oup.silverchair-cdn.com/oup/backfile/Content_public/Journal/evolut/77/12/10.1093_evolut_qpad160/3/m_qpad160_fig1.jpeg?Expires=1763470337&Signature=dgXV2aEUJ6XkJaQK-ORDPSLgFwwZJxsps4O1AMkQH0OifbCI9c9EJB8BBmLKVsCAo0gPcEFYHxEU1sZN48xYmxB0-K~HvhnbB-HubYP-a921j6tSrm-Itulk35yG-47CF7YwcgbLdcsk9YFaB-4gx1Oz~uZLo6TP589t5mF-2RqvQaKL3DfzAl7eUlbtOicaeS~TQ7MRMuzn1JCA~A5L2B6p-s9cHm8VIeBN1qQFNY~oQjwXABzr44R~cEh9nihRqAGGQM21mLedCvyUEbrAE0beI3bG7tM10B8qLg5x1AR54XcZrZpvd6KaZX82neT17cE8gcSUdJ5J0QkHCasg9w__&Key-Pair-Id=APKAIE5G5CRDK6RD3PGA) ## Some fun thoughts When we think about evolvability, we need to consider the mean of the population. . . . Even when multiple alternate strategies have are different fitness peaks with deep valleys between - the population may be able to contain both peaks. . . . Reproductive isolation due to alternate strategies requires the peaks to be far apart, or the valleys very deep. ## More consequences {.smaller} Whether populations can evolve to different parts of a fitness landscape depends on *how* the traits are correlated. . . . ![example](https://bio.libretexts.org/@api/deki/files/64592/clipboard_ed8dd74271e352ff1ddfeff98687f6ec8.png?revision=1&size=bestfit&width=637&height=350) ## Visually: Simulation courtesy of Diogo Melo: [link](https://curso-genevol.shinyapps.io/superficie-adaptativa/) ## Consequences for interpreting data. If a trait you are studying is controlled by many alleles, and is potentially linked to other traits under selection, inference of evolutionary patterns becomes increasingly difficult. . . . If the trait is highly polygenic, each individual allele might have low signal. . . . If the alleles controlling the trait are highly pleiotropic - signal may be dampened depending on how trait is measured. . . . If multiple traits genetically covariated and one under very strong selection - the other will have low polymorphism, so low power to detect causal alleles. ## The ultimate complex trait - fitness We've already mentioned this, but fitness is a highly composite trait. . . . Likely affected to some degree by more or less every allele *and* tied to most traits. . . . Yet, we can often detect clear signals of adaptation, with alleles showing strong relationships w/fitness. . . . So, even when you study complex traits, you *can* identify the causal alleles. But optimal values may be harder to find. ## Back to Speciation Let's consider for a moment two populations evolving to the _same_ peak. . . . Even though they will both evolve similar trait values, _how_ they control these traits may be different. . . . Simplest case: two traits, single optimum. . . . See chalkboard ## Speciation in Fisher's Geometric Model Fisher's Geometric Model can generate some nice predictions about how fitness between different groups will change as they diverge, _even if they evolve to the same peak_. . . . Notably - fitness in hybrids will decrease because of different combinations of alleles shifting you off of the optimum. . . . Cool aspects: - Makes relatively simple assumptions about the fitness landscape - Generates some known patterns of speciation biology - Can be parameterized using known hybrid fitness data - Can explain hybrid speciation Weaknesses: - Many more assumptions needed to get other classic results - Allows for heterosis, but only if parents are both unfit - Strong assumptions about the effect size of mutations, especially for some of the big results ## Alternatives to explain speciation Bateson-Dobzhansky-Muller Incompatibilities! . . . More on this next week, as we chat about all of the processes interplaying with each other for changes in allele frequencies. . . . The week after, we'll talk more about how the interplay of all of the processes results in trait evolution. . . . Finally, we'll chat about the geneology of all alleles including all of these processes - the Ancestral Recombination Graph. We'll discuss some approaches to estimating it, and what to do once you have it. ## Student's Choice The last two weeks we've reserved for student's choice of topics. . . . I'll send out a survey with several topics I would normally include but haven't had the time for, but I'll leave a blank for whatever your heart desires. . . . We'll lock in favorite options next week. . . . Strong caveat - if it's something I've never worked on, might not be as good of a lecture/lab. ## Paper for this week {.smaller} Chen and Pannell - completely optional, but cool study. . . . Examine how the fitness of different plants changes as they produce varying amounts of male/female flowers. . . . The optimum is _not_ to specialize in one or the other - indeed, the dynamics are quite complex. . . . Male flower production correlated with hermaphroditic flower production, so optimum becomes complex. . . . Further - self-fertilization can lead to inbreeding, so different optima depending on whether inbreeding is considered or ignored.
